title: Retro: Mixed-workload scheduler prototype (short/long prompt-aware scheduling)
content:
Date/time
- 2025-12-16 14:00–15:00 PT

Facilitator
- Talia Benson

Attendees (representative)
- Serving Runtime: Sofia, Lena, Marcus, Omar, Julian
- Kernels: Hiro, Grace, Yuki
- SRE/Obs: Sean, Allison, Rafael, Aisha
- Bench: Rina, Claire

Context / why we’re here
We shipped the short/long prompt-aware scheduler prototype (two-queue + aging + token budgets + prefill/decode separation hooks) behind a flag and ran it through benchmark-lab + perf-canary, then did a limited production canary in us-east on a subset of Dedicated pools. This retro is to capture what worked, what surprised us (especially kernel selection instability), and what we need to do if we want to graduate this beyond “prototype”.

Goals we set at kickoff (re-stated)
- Reduce user-visible p95 tail latency for short prompts under mixed prompt-length distributions (e.g., 80/20 short/long) without materially regressing throughput or creating starvation.
- Keep rollout safe: feature-flagged, observability in place, clear rollback triggers.

What went well
1) The policy change solved the actual pain we saw in traces
- In mixed scenarios the biggest win was reducing head-of-line blocking during long prefill bursts. The two-queue dispatch + token budgets made “short chat” traffic feel normal again while still making progress on long-context requests.
- Benchmarks (runtime-1.18 candidate) were directionally consistent with trace replay: short-class p95 and TTFT improved under 80/20 and long-spike mixes. We saw small throughput changes (generally low single digits) when tuned.

2) Aging/starvation guardrails were not optional, and we treated them as first-class
- The team found and fixed an actual long-queue starvation edge case during load tests (see pr-24905). Catching this pre-canary likely saved us a much nastier incident.
- The “max skew / burst cap” style constraints were very helpful for “unknown unknowns” during early tuning.

3) Prefill/decode separation hooks were a good architectural seam
- Even though we didn’t fully redesign the pipeline, moving to explicit hooks for prefill vs decode scheduling decisions reduced the worst cases where long-prefill dominated batch selection.
- It also made instrumentation easier to reason about (we could split time-in-queue and service time by phase).

4) Instrumentation and dashboards landed early enough to be useful
- Per-class queue depth, time-in-queue, dispatch share, starvation counters, and per-class p50/p95 made it possible to debug “why did p95 spike?” without guessing.
- The best debugging pattern during canary was: (a) confirm p95 movement, (b) check class mix + queue time, (c) confirm token budgets and any overruns, (d) correlate with kernel selection changes.

5) Rollout discipline was solid
- Feature flag + safe bounds for knobs (pr-24922) prevented “someone set short_share=1.0 at 2am” outcomes.
- SRE guardrails and a clear rollback plan reduced stress during the us-east canary window.

What surprised us / what we learned
1) Kernel selection instability showed up as a tail-latency amplifier
- The biggest surprise: when sequence length distribution shifts quickly (short/long interleaving), kernel auto-selection can “thrash” more than expected, which shows up as jitter in service time even if queueing is improved.
- This was especially visible during long-spike scenarios where the scheduler rapidly alternated between prefill-heavy and decode-heavy batches. The policy improved queue time but didn’t fully control the service-time variance.
- Takeaway: scheduler policy and kernel heuristics are coupled in mixed workloads. If we productize this, we likely need either (a) more stable kernel selection across nearby shapes, or (b) a scheduler-level constraint that reduces shape churn (at some cost).

2) KV-cache behavior interacted with “fairness” in non-obvious ways
- In some runs, protecting short traffic increased cache churn for long contexts (more interrupted long sequences). This occasionally showed up as cache eviction spikes and longer long-class completion time.
- The “correct” fairness definition depends on what we’re optimizing: request-level fairness vs token-level fairness vs TTFT fairness. We made pragmatic trade-offs for prototype, but it’s a product decision if we go further.

3) Metrics cardinality and interpretation issues
- Per-class metrics were great, but we had near-misses on label cardinality (pool/model/region + class + phase + error codes). We need a documented “allowed labels” set and a rollout checklist item to prevent this.
- Not all stakeholders interpret “p95 improved” the same way: Hosted cares about user-facing TTFT/p95, Dedicated cares about throughput predictability and “no surprises” during customer peaks.

4) Tuning knobs are more operationally sensitive than expected
- Small adjustments to token budgets and aging parameters changed results more than expected across SKUs.
- A single “default” probably won’t work across GPU types and model sizes without either (a) per-SKU defaults or (b) an auto-tuner / recommendation system.

5) Canary success criteria needed to be written down earlier
- We had rollback triggers, but we spent too much time during canary debating which metric mattered most (overall p95 vs short-class p95 vs long completion time, and which windows).
- Next time: a one-page “canary scorecard” aligned with PM + SRE should be in place before we flip any traffic.

What didn’t go well / pain points
- Debugging “service-time” regressions was slower than debugging queueing regressions. We needed kernel-level tracing sooner (and more guidance on how to interpret it under mixed workloads).
- We had a gap between benchmark-lab scenarios and production traffic spikes. The long-spike scenario helped, but we still under-modeled a couple real-world burst patterns (short traffic surge coincident with long-context batch jobs).
- Communication overhead: several parallel threads (#eng-runtime, #eng-sre, #eng-releases) made it easy to lose the current knob settings / canary state.

Decisions / agreements from retro
- We consider the prototype “successful enough” to keep iterating, but we do not want to default-enable broadly until kernel stability + KV-cache interactions are better understood.
- If we move toward productization, we need a combined scheduler+kernels plan rather than treating kernels as a downstream concern.

Action items (follow-ups for productization)
1) Kernel stability workstream (owner: Yuki Sato; support: Grace Kim; reviewer: Hiro Tanaka)
- Define what “kernel thrash” means operationally (metrics/trace signature + thresholds).
- Propose a mitigation: hysteresis in kernel selection, or a limited set of preferred kernels for mixed-mode batches.
- Deliverable: short design note + an experiment plan using the mixed workload bench suite.

2) KV-cache + fairness study (owner: Omar El-Sayed; reviewer: Lena Fischer)
- Analyze cache eviction / compaction events during mixed scheduling, correlate with long-class completion time regressions.
- Propose a guardrail (e.g., cap interruptions per long request, or minimum contiguous decode for long-class once scheduled).

3) “Canary scorecard” template + pre-flight checklist (owner: Sean Gallagher; partner: Aisha Bello; input: Paula Mendes)
- One pager that defines: success metrics, acceptable trade-offs, windows, rollback triggers, and required dashboards.
- Add this to the runbook as a required step before ramp.

4) Knob defaults + safe bounds per SKU/model (owner: Benji Okafor; partner: Rina Kobayashi)
- Write down current recommended defaults from runtime-1.18 results and what they’re conditioned on.
- Make it explicit which knobs are “operator safe” vs “engineer-only” (and where they can be set: pool vs model vs global).

5) Benchmark coverage gaps (owner: Claire Dubois)
- Add at least one scenario modeling: (a) short surge + long steady-state, and (b) periodic long-prefill spikes.
- Ensure we report not just p95/throughput but also long-class completion time distribution and starvation counters.

6) Observability hygiene (owner: Allison Grant)
- Document the required label set for scheduler metrics and a guideline for adding new labels.
- Confirm dashboards are discoverable from runtime metrics docs (link hygiene + “what to look at” notes).

7) Comms + state tracking during canary (owner: Connor O’Brien; partner: Rafael Mendes)
- Create a single canary status doc template: traffic %, knob config snapshot, links to dashboards, decision log.
- During the next ramp, we keep one “source of truth” instead of multiple Slack message edits.

Notes / quotes we should remember
- “Queueing was the obvious problem; service-time variance became the new bottleneck once queueing was fixed.”
- “Starvation prevention isn’t a feature—it’s a requirement.”
- “We can’t ship this as ‘scheduler-only’. Kernels and scheduler need to co-own mixed-mode behavior.”

Open questions (parking lot)
- Should we eventually move toward an SRPT-like approximation, or stick with two-queue + aging because it’s simpler to operate?
- How do we define fairness for Dedicated customers: per-request, per-token, or per-tenant? (Out of prototype scope, but productization will force the question.)
- Do we want the scheduler to be “model-aware” (different thresholds per model) by default, or only via config?

Appendix: quick pointers
- If you’re debugging mixed workload tail: start with per-class queue time + dispatch share, then look at kernel selection changes and cache eviction metrics.
- If long queue looks stuck: check starvation counters + aging rate; compare against the regression test added in pr-24905.
